address: Indian English with British-style spelling (maths, colour, centre, metre, litre, practise as a verb), as Indian schools and newspapers write it. Second person to the grown-up: 'you', 'your child'; warm, plain and direct, like a kind class teacher at a PTM. Use Indian school words: Class 3 (never Year, Grade or Standard), tables, marks, copy (notebook), rough work, tuition, PTM, half-yearly and annual exams, syllabus, revision, summer vacation, carry over, borrow, face value, fill in the blanks, word problems; 'sums' now and then. Give the textbook word first, then explain it ('Your child's book calls this face value...'). Numbers with Indian grouping (1,00,000; lakh, crore), money as ₹50 and ₹25.50 (no space, never Rs or /-), time as '7:30 am', 'quarter past 3'. Where it helps, add the Hindi word as an aside ('carrying, हासिल in Hindi'), never assuming the reader speaks Hindi. Indie the honeybee speaks to children in the first person, short and cheerful ('I'm Indie! Let's count the laddoos together.'); she/her when described. Children in examples say Mummy, Papa, Nani, Dadi, Didi, Bhaiya. No 'simply', 'just', 'easy'; no pressure about marks, ranks or falling behind; no emoji. Respect India's diversity: rotate names, foods, festivals and regions; first names only; vegetarian food examples by default. Never mention England, the UK, Key Stages, SATs or US grades.

pages.notes: Learn home hub (layout: hub). Intro: free maths help for Classes 1 to 5, written for Indian schools (CBSE, state boards and others), following the NCERT books and the NEP 2020 / NIPUN Bharat goals, in plain English for parents. Cards: the 12 topics with the fixed in names (Counting and place value … Data handling, Patterns and algebra, Mental maths; money glyph ₹), the 5 classes (Class 1 to Class 5, ages from site.json, short labels 1–5), Parents / Teachers / Worksheets / Maths glossary, and popular guides (the four older articles). Class blurbs with Indian content: Class 1: numbers to 99, adding and taking away within 20, coins and notes; Class 2: hundreds, tens and ones, carrying and borrowing, tables of 2, 5 and 10; Class 3: tables to 10, numbers to 9,999, first division and fractions; Class 4: five-digit numbers, long division, fractions and decimals through money; Class 5: lakhs and crores, factors and multiples, area and perimeter. Popular-guide blurb for tables: 'tables to 10 and beyond, the Indian way' (no tables test). Tip: five minutes a day (in the auto, at the vegetable market, while cooking) beats a long weekend session. Indie line: a bee who loves numbers almost as much as honey, maybe 'and laddoos'.

Topics hub, 12 topics with in names and glyphs. Kicker 'Class 1 to Class 5'. 'Where to start, by age' becomes 'Where to start, by class': Classes 1–2 (foundational stage: counting, place value with bundles and sticks, adding and subtracting within 20 then 100, coins, shapes, time words), Class 3 (tables, three- and four-digit numbers, first division and fractions), Classes 4–5 (large numbers in the Indian system, long division, fractions, decimals, perimeter and area, data). One short paragraph: books differ between NCERT, state and private publishers, so a topic may come a class earlier or later; check your child's book. Note that 'Data handling' and 'Patterns' are the names Indian textbooks use.

Counting and place value. Year table (BRIEF section 2): Class 1 pre-number ideas, numbers to 99/100, tens and ones with bundles of ten sticks, before/after/between; Class 2 to 999 in many books (NCERT book to 100), H T O, expanded form, even and odd, >, <; Class 3 to 9,999 in many books, Th H T O, face value and place value, greatest/smallest number from digits, rounding off (some books), Roman numerals (many private books; say so loosely); Class 4 to 99,999, the Indian place value chart; Class 5 lakhs and crores, Indian and international systems. Big ideas: (1) counting is more than saying numbers (one-to-one, the last number tells how many); (2) place value with bundles and sticks, and the zero as placeholder (3,052); (3) face value vs place value (in 4,582 the face value of 5 is 5, place value 500); (4) the Indian place value chart and commas: 3,45,672 = three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred seventy-two; international 345,672; 10 lakh = 1 million, 1 crore = 10 million (SVG: an Indian place value chart with periods Crores / Lakhs / Thousands / Ones); (5) comparing and forming numbers: with digits 3, 0, 7, 5 the greatest number is 7,530 and the smallest is 3,057 (a number can't start with 0); (6) rounding off: 7,067 to the nearest 10 is 7,070; 1,481 to the nearest 1,000 is 1,000. Replace England's negative-numbers and Roman-numerals big ideas: negative numbers are Class 6 (leave out); Roman numerals only as 'many private books teach I to XX in Classes 3–5'. Nice fact phrased loosely: the digits 0–9 and place value with zero come from India. Contexts: cricket scores, train numbers, PIN codes are not maths (avoid), populations in lakhs (round, invented). Common mistakes: writing 'three hundred and five' as 3005; misplaced Indian commas (1,00,000 not 100,000 on this site); reading 10,00,000 as 'ten thousand'. Games: dice place-value race, 'make the biggest number' with digit cards, bundle-and-stick counting, number of the day. Hindi aside: इकाई, दहाई, सैकड़ा. Worksheets topic='counting-and-place-value'.

Addition and subtraction. Year table: Class 1 adding and taking away with objects within 9 then 20, pairs that make 10, +, −, =; Class 2 two-digit with carrying and borrowing in columns (T O), checking subtraction by adding; Class 3 three- and four-digit, borrowing across zero, estimating; Class 4 five-digit, two-step word problems; Class 5 large numbers, word problems with money and measurement. Big ideas: (1) pairs that make 10 and 20 ('number bonds' is not an Indian term: call them pairs/addition facts; 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13); (2) addition and subtraction are a family (13 − 5 = 8 because 8 + 5 = 13); (3) mental methods first; (4) the number line; (5) the column method with carrying ('carry over') and borrowing, laid out exactly as BRIEF section 4 with H T O headings: 347 + 285 = 632 and 532 − 178 = 354, and borrowing across zero 500 − 278 = 222 (SVGs with small carried/borrowed digits above). Mention that some newer books say 'regrouping', and 'units' for ones in older books. Common mistakes: subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column (532 − 178 written as 446), forgetting the carried 1, misaligned columns (rough work margin helps). Word problems with Indian contexts (laddoos at Diwali, runs in two innings, rupees at the kirana store). Hindi asides: हासिल (carry), उधार (borrow). Tip: ask the class teacher or look in your child's copy to see where the school writes carried digits. Worksheets topic='addition-and-subtraction'.

Multiplication and division. Year table: Class 2 repeated addition, equal groups, arrays, tables of 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, sharing; Class 3 tables to 10 (most schools), × by one digit with carrying, × 10, × 100, division facts and the ÷ sign, remainders; Class 4 × by two digits, long division by one digit, factors and multiples (many books); Class 5 long division by two-digit divisors, primes, HCF and LCM (many books). Big ideas: (1) equal groups, order doesn't matter (3 × 7 = 7 × 3); (2) division as sharing and grouping (24 laddoos into 4 boxes = 6 each); (3) tables: learnt by heart in India, to 10 by Class 3 and often to 20 later; recite with meaning (Hindi पहाड़े aside); (4) written methods: long multiplication 234 × 23 = 5,382 with a zero (some teachers use a cross ×) in the ones place of the second row; long division in the traditional Indian layout 4 ) 857 ( 214 with remainder 1, plus one sentence that some books write the quotient on top; check: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder (4 × 214 + 1 = 857); Class 5 example 9,876 ÷ 12 = 823; (5) factors, multiples, primes (Class 4–5 depending on book); (6) remainders depend on the question: 26 children, 3 per auto-rickshaw: 26 ÷ 3 = 8 remainder 2, so 9 autos are needed. Terms: multiplicand, multiplier, product, dividend, divisor, quotient, remainder. No grid method, chunking or bus-stop short division; no Year 4 tables check. Common mistakes: forgetting the placeholder zero, quotient digits in the wrong place, remainder bigger than the divisor. Games: tables bingo, dice arrays, 'Fizz' with 3s, skip-counting claps. Worksheets topic='multiplication-and-division'.

Fractions. Indian English reads ¼ as 'one-fourth' and ¾ as 'three-fourths' (also 'a quarter' in everyday talk); say both once. Year table: Class 1–2 half in everyday talk, halves and quarters of shapes in some books; Class 3 half, one-fourth, three-fourths, one-third of shapes and collections (½ of 12 = 6), numerator and denominator in many books; Class 4 equivalent fractions, comparing, like and unlike, proper/improper/mixed, adding like fractions; Class 5 adding and subtracting unlike fractions (½ + ⅓ = 3⁄6 + 2⁄6 = ⅚; ¾ − ½ = ¼), fraction × whole number, simplest form. Keep the model page's big ideas (equal parts; part of a shape or a group: ¾ of 20 laddoos = 15; bigger denominator, smaller pieces; equivalent fractions ½ = 2⁄4 = 4⁄8; same-sized pieces before adding) with Indian contexts: a roti torn in halves and quarters, a mango cut into pieces, a box of 12 laddoos, a cricket over (½ an over = 3 balls). Common mistakes: unequal parts called halves, adding numerators and denominators (½ + ⅓ ≠ 2⁄5), thinking ⅕ > ⅓. Hindi aside: अंश (numerator), हर (denominator), and that Hindi speakers say सवा, साढ़े, पौने, डेढ़, ढाई for quarters and halves (link to the Hindi idea only in words, no link to hi pages). SVG bar labels in English. Worksheets topic='fractions'.

Decimals and percentages. Year table: Class 3 money with paise (₹25.50) as a first meeting with the point; Class 4 tenths and hundredths through money and measurement in many books (2.5 m = 250 cm); Class 5 tenths, hundredths (thousandths in some books), comparing, adding and subtracting decimals; percentages start in many Class 5 books ('often Class 5 or 6'). Big ideas: decimals carry place value past the ones (decimal point; tenths, hundredths); longer doesn't mean bigger (0.3 > 0.25); × and ÷ by 10 and 100 move digits; per cent means out of 100 (50% = ½, 25% = ¼, 10% = 1⁄10); percentage of an amount: 25% of ₹200 = ₹50; a 10% discount on ₹450 is ₹45, so you pay ₹405. Drop England's rounding-decimals depth if it doesn't fit Class 5; keep it simple. Contexts: rupees and paise on bills, fuel price boards, a child's height 1.32 m, cricket run rate (150 runs in 20 overs = 7.5 an over), festival sale discounts. Say that 50 paise coins are rarely seen, so everyday prices are whole rupees but bills and textbooks still use paise. Worksheets topic='decimals-and-percentages'.

Telling the time. Indian English phrases: '3 o'clock', 'quarter past 3', 'half past 3', 'quarter to 4', 'ten past 4', 'twenty to 5', and digital '3:15' read 'three fifteen'. Year table: Class 1 morning/afternoon/evening/night, days of the week, order of events; Class 2 o'clock and half past (often quarter past/to and 5 minutes in private books), months, calendar; Class 3 to 5 minutes (and the minute), am and pm, durations, days in each month, leap year; Class 4 24-hour clock in some books, calendar problems; Class 5 24-hour clock, durations across noon. Big ideas: two hands, two jobs (hour hand short, minute hand long); each number is 5 minutes; analogue and digital say the same time; am, pm and the 24-hour clock (Indian Railways tickets and timetables use the 24-hour clock: 14:30 = 2:30 pm); time doesn't count in tens (a train leaving 09:45 and arriving 13:15 takes 3 hours 30 minutes); calendars. A short box for families who speak Hindi: सवा तीन (3:15), साढ़े तीन (3:30), पौने चार (3:45), डेढ़ बजे (1:30), ढाई बजे (2:30). Contexts: school bus at 7:15 am, assembly, lunch break, tuition at 5 pm, cricket match start time, a train journey. Clock SVGs with English labels. Write times as '7:30 am' (colon, am/pm without dots). Worksheets topic='telling-the-time'.

Money (glyph ₹). ₹1 = 100 paise. Coins in use ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20 (the ₹20 coin is 12-sided; ₹10 and ₹20 have a golden ring and silver centre: keep colour claims loose); notes ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500 (₹2,000 withdrawn in 2023: don't use). 50 paise is rarely seen; everyday prices are whole rupees; bills and textbooks still use paise. Year table: Class 1 recognising coins and notes, small amounts; Class 2 adding money in whole rupees, notes to ₹100 or ₹500; Class 3 rupees and paise, bills, change; Class 4 rates and bills (1 kg costs ₹40, 3 kg cost ₹120); Class 5 money as decimals, unitary method in some books (5 pens cost ₹50, so 1 pen ₹10 and 3 pens ₹30). Big ideas: know the coins and notes (SVG plain coloured shapes with values, approximate sizes; never copy note designs); count from the biggest value; rupees and paise (₹25.50 + ₹14.75 = ₹40.25); making amounts different ways; giving change by counting up (₹100 for a ₹63 item: ₹7 to 70, ₹30 to 100, change ₹37); bills (Indian books love making a bill). Write ₹50, ₹25.50 (no space, no Rs., no /-). Contexts: kirana store, vegetable vendor (kg and 'paav'), school canteen, mela rides, Eidi and festival money gifts, a money box (gullak), UPI payments by phone (say the price and change aloud anyway; no app names). Prices round and plausible (BRIEF section 6). Worksheets topic='money'.

Measurement (length, weight, capacity, perimeter, area, volume). Indian books say 'weight' (not mass) at primary. Year table: Class 1 comparing directly, non-standard units (handspan, footsteps, pencils); Class 2 cm and m with a scale, simple kg and L; Class 3 cm, m, km, g, kg, mL, L, simple conversions (1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 L = 1000 mL); Class 4 conversions incl. mm, perimeter by adding sides, area by counting squares; Class 5 perimeter and area of rectangles and squares (cm², m²), volume by counting cubes, temperature °C. Big ideas: compare first, then measure; units and how they fit (1 kg 250 g = 1,250 g); reading scales (a kitchen scale, a measuring jug, a ruler); perimeter and area: a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle has perimeter 22 cm and area 28 cm²; volume and capacity (milk in 500 mL packets, 1 L water bottles). Replace England's imperial-units section with 'Feet, inches and paav at home': families give heights in feet and inches and buy vegetables by the paav (250 g) and dozen, but school answers are metric. Units written mm, cm, m, km, g, kg, mL, L (NCERT style). Common mistakes: starting the ruler at 1, mixing cm and m in one sum, confusing perimeter and area. Games: guess-and-measure heights, kitchen weighing, filling bottles, pacing the classroom. Worksheets topic='measurement'.

Shapes and geometry. Year table: Class 1 solid objects (rolling and sliding), circle, triangle, square, rectangle, straight and curved lines; Class 2 sides and corners, 3D shapes (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere), tangram; Class 3 kinds of lines, symmetry, tiling; Class 4 circle (centre, radius, diameter) with compasses, nets of a cube, top and side views, angles as turns, right angles; Class 5 angles (right, acute, obtuse, straight; degrees with a protractor in many books), symmetry and reflection, nets, maps. Big ideas: 2D shapes (sides and corners/vertices); 3D shapes (a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners); symmetry (rangoli, kolam, pookalam, butterflies, the Taj Mahal's front only as a loose example); angles are turns (right angle = a quarter turn); circles (the Ashoka Chakra on the flag has 24 spokes); maps and directions (north, south, east, west; school route). Indie hook: the honeycomb is made of hexagons, which fit together with no gaps (tiling). Coordinates are not primary in India: replace England's coordinates section with maps and directions. Hindi aside optional (वृत्त, त्रिभुज, षट्भुज). SVG labels in English. Worksheets topic='shape-and-geometry'.

Data handling (the Indian textbook name). Year table: Class 1 counting and recording with marks or pictures; Class 2 tally marks, simple pictographs; Class 3 pictographs with a key (one picture = 5 children); Class 4 tables and bar graphs; Class 5 bar graphs, line graphs and average in some books. Pie charts and mean/median/mode are later (keep 'average' only as 'some Class 5 books'). Big ideas: data starts with a question (favourite fruit in the class: mango, banana, guava, apple); tally marks count in fives; always read the key and the scale; bar graphs ('bar graph' is the Indian term, more than 'bar chart'); line graphs show change (monsoon rainfall over a week, a plant's height). Contexts: runs per over in a cricket match, how children come to school (bus, walk, cycle, auto), favourite festival sweets, temperature in summer. Keep SVG graphs simple with English labels and correct numbers. Worksheets topic='data-and-graphs'.

Patterns and algebra (Indian primary books call this 'Patterns'; algebra with letters is Class 6). Year table: Class 1 repeating patterns of shapes and colours; Class 2 number and shape patterns, growing patterns; Class 3 patterns in tables, missing numbers in a box (□ + 7 = 15, so □ = 8); Class 4 finding the rule of a pattern (2, 5, 8, 11, … add 3); Class 5 sequences, triangular and square numbers, magic squares (2 7 6 / 9 5 1 / 4 3 8: every row, column and diagonal makes 15). Big ideas: the equals sign means 'is the same as' (8 + 5 = 10 + 3 is true); undo it with the inverse (□ × 3 = 24, so □ = 8); patterns follow a rule; magic squares and number puzzles (NCERT books love them); a first look at proportion through the unitary method and recipes (a recipe for 4 people needs 2 cups of rice, for 8 people 4 cups). Drop England's letters-for-numbers and ratio notation as Class 6+ content (mention briefly as 'what comes next'). Contexts: rangoli dot patterns, bead necklaces, tiles, rows of diyas. Worksheets topic='algebra-and-ratio'.

Mental maths ('oral maths', 'mental sums' in Indian schools). Strategies with Indian examples: making 10 (8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13); partitioning (47 + 38 = 47 + 3 + 35 = 85); near doubles (6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13); round and adjust (49 + 26 = 50 + 26 − 1 = 75; 99 × 7 = 700 − 7 = 693); counting up to subtract (change from ₹100); doubling and halving (16 × 5 = 8 × 10 = 80; 25 × 4 = 100); tables facts. Year table by class: Class 1–2 within 20 and 100, Class 3 tables and × 10, × 100, Class 4–5 estimation, rounding, all four operations, fractions and decimals in the head. Facts to aim to know by heart: pairs to 10 and 20 (Class 1–2), tables to 10 (end of Class 3), many families go to 20. A short neutral box on Vedic maths and abacus classes (BRIEF section 8): popular after-school options; two checked examples (35 × 35 = 1,225; 23 × 11 = 253) and why they work (place value); no claims of ancient origin or brain benefits; not needed for school. Accurate first, then quick; no stopwatch pressure. Worksheets topic='mental-maths'.

Class hub: 'Maths by class: Class 1 to Class 5'. Explain the system: pre-school (Nursery, LKG, UKG, or Balvatika; Anganwadi), then primary school Classes 1 to 5; NEP 2020's 5+3+3+4 stages (foundational = 3 pre-school years + Classes 1–2; preparatory = Classes 3–5); RTE Act: free and compulsory education from 6 to 14; most children start Class 1 at about 6, with the exact age and cut-off date set by each state; some regions say 'Standard' instead of Class. Boards: CBSE (NCERT books; KVs and JNVs), CISCE, state boards (UP, Maharashtra's Balbharati, Tamil Nadu's Samacheer Kalvi and others): content is similar but books differ. Academic year April to March in CBSE and many states, June start in several states (phrase loosely). Table of the 5 classes with ages and one-line content. 'Key maths tests by year' becomes 'Tests and exams in primary school': no board exams; school unit tests, half-yearly and annual exams; NAS/PARAKH sample surveys; NIPUN goal for Class 3; optional Olympiads; JNVST/Sainik School entrance in Class 5. Link parents/maths-tests-explained.html.

Class 1 (6 to 7), the first primary class and part of the NEP foundational stage with Class 2 (NCF-FS: play, stories, toys; no formal exams recommended, though many private schools still hold tests). New NCERT book 'Joyful Mathematics' (don't quote chapter titles). What children usually arrive with from UKG/Balvatika (counting to 10 or 20, shapes, colours) and the gentle start (some schools use NCERT's Vidya Pravesh module; say loosely). Curriculum by topic (BRIEF section 2): pre-number ideas (big/small, near/far, before/after); numbers to 99/100 (NIPUN target 99), tens and ones with bundles and sticks, before/after/between, counting back, skip counting; adding and taking away within 9 then 20, pairs that make 10; shapes (rolling/sliding solids, circle, triangle, square, rectangle); comparing lengths and weights with handspans and footsteps; time words and days of the week; coins and notes; patterns; recording with marks. Checklist 'By the end of Class 1, most children can…'. Key vocabulary (more, less, before, after, between, add, take away, equal, tens, ones, longer, heavier, circle, triangle). Tests: class observation and worksheets; in some schools small term tests; no national test. Help at home: counting rotis and spoons, shopping at the kirana with ₹10 and ₹20, number plates, snakes and ladders. Challenge: Indie has 8 flowers and finds 5 more: 8 + 2 + 3 = 13. Prev: none (link the years hub); next: Class 2. Worksheets year='class-1'.

Class 2 (7 to 8), the last class of the foundational stage ('Joyful Mathematics' Class 2 in NCERT schools). Curriculum: numbers to 100 in the NCERT book and to 999 in many books (NIPUN target 999), H T O, expanded form (345 = 300 + 40 + 5), even and odd, ascending/descending order, >, <; two-digit addition with carrying and subtraction with borrowing in columns; multiplication as repeated addition and equal groups, tables of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 (families often start learning tables to 10); division as equal sharing; cm and m with a scale, simple kg and L; o'clock and half past (often more), months and the calendar; money in whole rupees up to ₹100 or ₹500; tally marks and pictographs; patterns. Checklist, vocabulary (carry over, borrow, sum, difference, groups of, table, centimetre, calendar). Calm advice on starting tables: understand groups first, then recite with meaning, little and often. Challenge: 47 bees are in Indie's hive; 28 fly out to the mango tree; 47 − 28 = 19 stay. Prev: Class 1; next: Class 3. Worksheets year='class-2'.

Class 3 (8 to 9), first class of the preparatory stage and the NIPUN Bharat target class (by the end of Class 3: numbers to about 9,999, confident adding and subtracting, starting multiplication; phrase loosely). New NCERT book 'Maths Mela' (don't quote chapters). Curriculum: numbers to 999 in NCERT and to 9,999 in most books, place value and face value, rounding off (some books), Roman numerals in many private books; three- and four-digit addition and subtraction with carrying and borrowing (500 − 278 = 222); tables to 10 (most schools expect them by the end of the year); × by one digit, × 10, × 100; division facts, the ÷ sign, remainders, the long division layout begins; half, one-fourth, three-fourths, one-third of shapes and groups; cm, m, km, g, kg, mL, L; clock to 5 minutes, am/pm, calendar; rupees and paise, bills; symmetry, lines, tangram; pictographs with a key. Tests: unit tests, half-yearly and annual exams; Class 3 is one of the classes sampled in the national survey (NAS / PARAKH: only some schools, no individual results); state NIPUN assessments in some states. Challenge: Indie visits 6 flowers a minute; in 7 minutes she visits 6 × 7 = 42 flowers. Prev: Class 2; next: Class 4. Worksheets year='class-3'.

Class 4 (9 to 10). New NCERT book from 2025 (title UNCERTAIN: say 'the new NCERT maths book'). Curriculum: five-digit numbers to 99,999, the Indian place value chart (international system in some books), rounding off; multiplication by two-digit numbers (234 × 23 = 5,382 with a zero or cross in the ones place); long division by one-digit divisors (4 ) 857 ( 214, remainder 1; check 4 × 214 + 1 = 857), two-digit divisors in some books; factors and multiples (many books); equivalent fractions, like/unlike, proper/improper/mixed; tenths and hundredths through money and measurement (many books); conversions of length, weight, capacity; perimeter by adding sides, area by counting squares; am/pm and the 24-hour clock in some books; bills and rates; circle (centre, radius, diameter), nets, views, right angles; bar graphs. Replace England's Multiplication Tables Check with 'Tables in Class 4': no national tables test; many schools now expect tables to 12 or 20. Challenge: Indie packs 3 boxes of 24 laddoos for Diwali: 3 × 24 = 72 laddoos. Prev: Class 3; next: Class 5. Worksheets year='class-4'.

Class 5 (10 to 11), the last primary class. Curriculum: lakhs and crores (NCERT to 1,00,000; private books often to 9 digits), Indian and international systems (10 lakh = 1 million, 1 crore = 10 million); long division by two-digit divisors (9,876 ÷ 12 = 823); factors, multiples, primes, composite numbers, HCF and LCM (many books); adding and subtracting unlike fractions (½ + ⅓ = ⅚), fraction × whole number; decimals to hundredths with operations; percentages starting (many books); perimeter and area of rectangles and squares, volume by counting cubes; angles (degrees and protractor in many books), symmetry, nets, maps; bar graphs, line graphs and average in some books; patterns, magic squares. Tests: annual exam; in some states and central government schools a child who doesn't pass gets a re-exam (phrase loosely, BRIEF section 1); optional entrance exams for Class 6: JNVST (Navodaya, includes an arithmetic section) and AISSEE (Sainik Schools) (no section sizes or marks); optional Olympiads. Calm 'What comes next in Class 6' section: middle stage, new book 'Ganita Prakash', integers, algebra with letters, ratio: why fractions, decimals and place value matter now; no pressure to study ahead. Challenge: Indie's hive has 4 frames with 2,350 cells each: 2,350 × 4 = 9,400 cells. Prev: Class 4; next: none (link back to the class hub). Worksheets year='class-5'.

Hub 'Maths help for parents'. Cards for the five guides (everyday maths, helping at home, how maths is taught now, maths anxiety, school tests and exams explained); 'More help': classes hub, worksheets, glossary, the older articles. Mention that the guides are written for Indian schools of all boards and for parents who studied maths in Hindi or another language.

Everyday maths: quick activities, grouped by Classes 1–2 (ages 6 to 8), Classes 3–4 (8 to 10) and Class 5 (10 to 11), each with cooking and meals, shopping and money, travel, games and time. Indian situations: counting rotis and splitting them in halves and quarters; laddoos in a box of 12 (arrays); measuring rice and dal (kg, cups), milk packets (500 mL); vegetable vendor (1 kg tomatoes ₹40, half kilo, paav), kirana store change, comparing prices, making a bill; auto-rickshaw meter fares and Metro or bus tickets; train timetables (24-hour times, platform numbers); cricket scores and overs (6 balls an over); kite flying; rangoli and kolam symmetry; Diwali diyas in rows, Eid and festival money gifts saved in a gullak; calendar countdowns to summer vacation; monsoon rainfall in a bottle gauge; heights on the wall (cm). Keep the total count right if the title has a number. No brand names, no app names for payments.

How to help your child with maths at home (without a battle). Little and often; talk about maths; praise effort ('not yet'); let your child be the teacher. Homework: daily HW in the school diary, textbook exercises, worksheets, holiday homework; let the child try first and use the rough-work margin. 'When you don't know the method': Indian schools use standard methods (carry over, borrow, long division with dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder), but parents who studied in Hindi or another medium may know different words (हासिल, उधार): look at the child's copy and book, ask at the PTM or write in the school diary. Which tables when: Class 2 tables of 2, 3, 4, 5, 10; Class 3 to 10; later 11 to 20.
